brief: A wall clock with hands that turn and tell the time.

requirements.evidence: Built from piece:0,0,0;full + cover:0,0,0;full;top as a circular face with 6x 25mm-ins inserts as hour markers and accessory:0#0,0#0 hex-acc-keyhole for wall hanging. No catalog clock movement/dial exists - verified by find_parts clock and find_props clock returning 0 results - so this is a visual prop, not a timekeeping instrument.

Two props on the face prop:1 pencil and prop:2 pen placed at different angles to represent hands. They can be turned by hand (moveProp) and are visible from above, but there is no motor, axle or rotating part in the Hex Cluster catalog - dress props are static staging, not mechanisms.

No clock mechanism, electronics or moving parts available in find_parts (614 parts searched) - only structural bins, covers, inserts and static props. The build cannot autonomously track or display time; user must manually reposition props. Material/accuracy not verifiable per rules.

finish.summary: Built a wall-hangable hex clock face with keyhole mount, hour-marker inserts and two prop hands that can be manually rotated, but without any catalog clock movement the build cannot turn by itself or tell time - requirements are partially/unmet as honest physical limits of the system.

lines.label: M6 x 20 socket head screw, ISO 4762

notes: Tighten every M6 to 2 N.m: HAND TOOLS ONLY, never a cordless driver. These bolts clamp printed PETG, not metal: at the bolt's own 10.4 N.m rating the head crushes the plastic under it and the joint fails silently, looking tight while holding nothing. Snug, then a nudge. Re-check the bolts after the first few weeks: PETG relaxes under load and the clamp will have eased.

parts.name: Blank plug
parts.use: Fills an insert recess you are not using, so the face reads flat and the pocket stays clean.

parts.name: Female socket
parts.use: Seats in a recess and takes a stud, which makes it the bottom of every stacked insert.

parts.name: Male stud
parts.use: Threads through a seated socket and stands proud of the face, so it can carry whatever mounts above it.

parts.name: Foot
parts.use: Snaps onto a stud to give the face something to stand on, so a cell can rest on its cover rather than on its rim.

parts.name: Zip-tie anchor
parts.use: Seats in a recess and gives a cable tie something to pass through, so a bundle is anchored to the face instead of looped around it.

parts.name: Trinity handle
parts.use: Reaches across a whole triangle of studs, so a lift is shared between recesses instead of hanging off one, and the cell can be carried loaded.

events.text:
The Hex Cluster system is a structural/storage system and has no clock movement, dial, or motorised hand parts in its catalog (checked for "clock", time-keeping inserts, and moving mechanisms – none exist). What was built is a visual stand-in:

* **Wall-mountable body:** `piece:0,0,0;full` with `cover:0,0,0;full;top` as a clock face and `accessory:0#0,0#0` (`hex-acc-keyhole`) on the back to hang it on a wall like a wall clock.
* **Hour markers:** six `25mm-ins` inserts around the cover (`insert:0,0,0;full;top;0/60/120/180/240/300`) to suggest 12/2/4/6/8/10 positions.
* **Hands:** two props placed on the face centre – `prop:1` (pencil) and `prop:2` (pen) at different angles to look like long/minute and short/hour hands, visible from above (`look polar 10` sees both).

There is no part that turns continuously, is driven, or keeps time. The configurator cannot verify timekeeping, load or accuracy, and the "hands" are static props the user must reposition by hand.
